message:
Recent avalanche activity north of Crested Butte is a good indication of what's coming on Wednesday, and gives us concern that dangerous conditions may return by the weekend.

In a few isolated areas that received about 6 inches of new snow over the weekend, observers reported numerous small loose-snow avalanches and one larger storm slab avalanche.

A widespread layer of Surface Hoar resting on soft facets sits only a few inches below the snow surface. Since the weak layer formed (early November) and was preserved under a soft cap of fresh snow (last weekend), we've known there's a lurking time bomb in the upper snowpack. Tuesday night's new snow and strong winds will build thin slabs in the driftiest spots, and make it easy for you to trigger a small avalanche in those spots on Wednesday.

Looking ahead, the storm expected Friday into Saturday may be enough to dramatically change the danger. If the forecast snow totals hold, we expect slab volume to grow, making avalanches larger, and spreading the danger onto more slopes, further from ridgelines. Stay tuned.

Images.caption: A small amount of recent snow has buried and preserved a delicate weak layer. The thin layer just below the new snow is buried surface hoar, which can be particularly nasty once a thicker slab builds on top.
Images.altText: A black glove next to a small snow pit

Images.caption: This fresh Storm Slab avalanche is a good indication of what's in store when we get more snow and wind. Many slopes on the north half of the compass have a buried weak layer, just waiting for a more connected slab to set things off.
Images.altText: A fresh slab avalanche below a rocky face

Images.caption: Watch for small avalanches like these in steep, shady terrain, especially as we get more snow. They may not bury you, but they can knock you down into rockier terrain below.
Images.altText: Small loose snow avalanches below a ridge

message:
The Southern Mountains were the winners in the state for the recent storm, with new snow totals mostly in the five to seven inch range. The snow was accompanied by strong south and southwest wind, so we're also the winners in the increased danger category. While reported avalanches are on the small side, many have been remotely triggered. This is a good indication of the widespread weak layer that is now buried. Tomorrow is another break between storms, and a great opportunity to poke around and get some observations prior to the Thursday/Friday event, which also promises to be windy. The incoming storm looks to be colder than this seasons previous storms. Expect the snowline to creep lower in elevation and avalanche size to increase with each incremental loading event.

Pay close attention to changing conditions, as we are amidst a string of unsettled weather.

Images.caption: The snowpack is deep for this time of the year in the San Juan Mountains. This photo from the Wilson Group outside of Telluride shows just how caked the mountains look. These folks also found more than 2 meters of snow on the ground on a northwest-facing slope above treeline. Snow cover becomes patchy at lower elevations and on the eastern edge of the Southern Mountains.

The last snowfall event was on November 2nd, and since then, high pressure weather has weakened the snow surface. We now have widespread near-surface facets and surface hoar on top of the snowpack, which became our first buried weak layer of the season.

message:
Colorado has had little snow in November, but we did get our first significant wind event Wednesday morning. An unusual amount of snow was on west aspects before the wind started to blow, so keep an eye out for newly developed drifts of firm snow that could result in a small Wind Slab avalanche, especially in very steep terrain.

The snow on the ground is very weak, and in the Flat Tops and Park Range it may have been capped by a thin layer of snow on Wednesday morning. These areas picked up a couple of inches of snow. Although there isn't enough slab to be a concern right now, a potential foot of new snow in these areas on Friday could increase avalanche danger. When the snow surface is very weak, as it is now, it often doesn’t take much slab to cause small avalanches.

In other areas keep an eye on what elevations and aspects are currently holding continuous snow. This snow is weak and will become a buried layer of concern when the storms start rolling in.

Images.caption: Looking west from the top of Loveland Pass on November 15. You can see there isn't quite enough snow to overcome surface roughness on these north-, northeast-, and east-facing slopes, but maybe enough to form a weak layer in the future.
Images.altText: A rounded alpine ridge with patchy snow cover

Images.caption: The north-facing slopes of Red Peak from Hoosier Pass on November 12. This is one of the snowier areas in the Northern Mountains right now.
This image from the Sentinel Weekly satellite on Caltopo shows the patchy snow cover age in the Northern Mountains. These areas of white are thin and patchy, but also weak and faceted.
Images.altText: A satellite image showing thin strips of snow in the Northern Mountains and a whole lot of greenery.
